Mission Model

A mission-performance simulator that sweeps every motor, propeller, and battery combination it is given. The model runs a theoretical mission, the DARPA 2028 heavy lift, and returns the feasibility of each combination. It's state based, with the states of landed, take-off, transition, cruise, and land. The model runs a system of dynamics equations to model the motion of flight in every state except transition. In the transition state the drone uses a quaternion model to better represent its motion through the transition from vertical to horizontal flight.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
Mission Model simulates the running of a course for a variety of airframes. The current iteration runs the following mission: takeoff to 100 ft, cruise 1 nautical mile, land, pick up cargo, takeoff, cruise 8 nm, land, drop cargo, takeoff, cruise 1 nm back, land. For every candidate airframe, it sweeps every motor × propeller × battery combination it has spec data for and reports which one actually completes the mission. It also reports back how much battery it has left over, and how long it can hover.

The airframe list (Hexacopter, Quadcopter, x8, Tail Sitter) matches the real vehicle classes I work on as Mechanical and Aerospace Team Lead on the VTOL team. This is the same kind of simulation-to-inform-design work as the MATLAB/Python scripts I write for the team, built out as a standalone public tool.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
Every TailSitter vehicle config is sized using Wing Optimizer's energy-based (hover + cruise) objective, evaluated at each tier's real governed cruise speed. The required wing area scales as 1/v², so getting the real cruise speed right has a large impact on the sizing result.

Hover time

Hover is the baseline number in the fleet chart. Each motor holds its share of the total mass, so I solve the motor's thrust curve for the throttle that does it, then divide the battery capacity by the current the whole rotor set draws at that throttle.

Hover throttle and endurance
Tm(θh)=mtotNthover=60·CAhN·I(θh)min

Tm is one motor's thrust curve, N the rotor count, CAh the battery capacity, and I the per-motor current. I find θh on 40–100% throttle with Brent's method against the continuous curve. If a motor can't reach mtot/N even at full throttle, hover time is zero.

One equation for every takeoff and every multirotor leg

A takeoff, and every leg a wingless multirotor flies, is the same differential equation: constant thrust against quadratic drag. It has an exact tanh solution, so every accel or decel leg is solved in one evaluation instead of stepped through a simulation loop.

Thrust against quadratic drag
dvdt=a0−kv2k=ρCdA2m a0=T−Wm(takeoff)a0=T2−W2m(multirotor cruise)
Closed-form solution
v(t)=vttanh(kvtt+c0)x(t)=lncosh(kvtt+c0)−lncosh(c0)k vt=a0kc0=artanh(v0vt)

vt is the terminal velocity where thrust and drag balance. Each leg stops at whichever comes first, the target speed or the distance cap. Reaching v* takes t = [artanh(v*/vt) − c0]/(k·vt), and covering a distance d takes ud = arcosh(cosh c0 · ekd). I compute ln cosh x as |x| − ln 2 + ln(1 + e−2|x|) so an underpowered vehicle with a large k·d doesn't overflow.

Cruise speed is an output of the throttle

I don't prescribe a cruise speed. Each leg settles at the speed where drag balances the forward thrust the throttle leaves over. Tilting the rotors to push forward costs weight support, so forward thrust is what remains after supporting the weight the wing doesn't carry, and the tilt inflates the frontal area that drag sees.

Equilibrium speed under tilt and wing lift
Th=T2−(W−L)2L=12ρCLSv2 Aeff=ATTh+CD0SCdTh=12ρCdAeffveq2

I solve the right-hand equation for veq with Brent's method, and fly each leg at min(0.995·veq, vmax). The cap vmax is 18 m/s (about 35 kt): a bare thrust-drag balance comes out at triple-digit speeds for these small frontal areas, which no cargo VTOL in this weight class will fly.

Braking uses the rotors

The decel leg is the accel equation with the thrust pointed the other way, so it has a closed form too. I first let the vehicle coast down on drag alone, but a coast takes time proportional to 1/k, so a lower-drag vehicle took longer to finish a leg. That's backwards for a VTOL that can brake with its rotors.

Powered braking down to the approach speed
dvdt=−(a0+kv2)b=a0k x=12klna0+kv02a0+kvf2t=arctan(v0/b)−arctan(vf/b)kb

v0 is the cruise speed the leg starts from, and vf is the 1 m/s landing-approach floor.

Energy and feasibility

Battery use is current times time, with the current read off the same throttle curve as the thrust. A configuration is feasible if the legs together stay inside the battery's rated capacity. Energy adds across legs and no leg's time budget constrains another, so maximizing leftover energy is the same as minimizing each of the six powered legs (three takeoffs, three cruises) on its own. That turns one joint throttle search into six one-dimensional sweeps over 40–100% throttle.

Per-leg energy and the feasibility test
Eleg=N·I(θ)·tleg3600∑legsEleg≤Crated

E in mAh. Landing isn't optimized: descent is prescribed at 5 m/s down to 10 ft and 1 m/s below that, drawing the 40%-throttle current scaled linearly to 30% and then 20% throttle. The payload rides the outbound 8 nm leg only.

The limit I know about: capacity is the rated mAh, flat. Peukert derating is a lead-acid effect that barely touches Li-ion at drone C-rates, but voltage sag under load can trip the cutoff before the rated capacity is drawn. For a high-current or aged pack I'd expect roughly 10–30% less usable capacity. That range is an order-of-magnitude estimate from hobbyist sources, and modeling it properly needs internal-resistance data I don't have.

The transition leg

A winged tailsitter's hover-to-cruise transition can't take that shortcut. The rotor thrust has to physically rotate from vertical to horizontal as the wing builds lift with airspeed, so the required thrust angle and the drag area both keep changing through the maneuver. I integrate that leg as a full quaternion 6DOF rigid body, position, velocity, attitude, and angular rate together. Attitude kinematics: q̇ = ½ q ⊗ [0, ω] (Hamilton, scalar-first), alongside the rotational dynamics I ω̇ = τ − ω × (Iω). I use quaternions specifically because Euler angles hit a gimbal-lock singularity right at the 90° pitch-over a tailsitter transition goes through.

Lift points along the wing's own body-fixed axis and scales with the velocity component perpendicular to it, rather than pointing straight up and scaling with raw airspeed the way a simpler model would. That distinction matters most mid-transition, when the vehicle is neither purely hovering nor purely cruising and a fixed lift direction isn't a safe approximation.

Attitude controller, lift direction, and inertia
e=log(q−1⊗qtarget)τ=clip(kpIe−kdIω,±τmax) L→=12ρCLS|v⊥|2a^v⊥=v−(v·a^)a^ Ix=m(0.25b2)2Iy=m(0.35l2)2Iz=Ix+Iy

The log map returns the shortest-path rotation vector, an angle of 2·atan2(|v|, w) wrapped to ±π. The lift axis â is the body −x axis, which points straight up at cruise attitude and edge-on at hover. Inertia comes from Roskam's radii of gyration for light aircraft (b is wingspan, l is body length), and τmax is the single-motor thrust range times a half-length arm, with yaw authority set to 20% of pitch. Those are estimates until CAD gives real principal moments, and I can override them per vehicle. I integrate with an adaptive solver (rtol 1e-6, max step 0.5 s) until forward speed reaches the target or the distance cap.

Wing Optimizer

A wing-sizing tool that searches lift coefficient, aspect ratio, and taper ratio for whichever combination minimizes structural mass, cruise drag, or total mission energy. Three of its search objectives are grounded in real aerostructural optimization papers. It doesn't claim to replicate methods like RANS CFD, nonlinear FE, or flight test. A standalone script can't actually run those.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
wing_optimizer.py sizes a wing from mission requirements alone. It takes how much weight the wing has to lift and how fast the aircraft cruises, then searches lift coefficient, aspect ratio, and (for the energy objective) taper ratio for whichever combination minimizes structural mass, cruise drag, or total mission energy. It emits the winning geometry as SolidWorks-ready NACA equations or point-cloud curves, plus a vehicle_configs-style JSON entry Mission Model can load directly.

Three of its objectives are each grounded in one real aerostructural optimization paper. The method below covers what carried over from each paper, and what I deliberately left out of scope.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
Aerodynamic-center reporting is inspired by Grimm, Price & Ahmad's flight-tested flying-wing optimization (Aerospace Systems, 2026), which treats longitudinal stability as the primary design objective. wing_mac_and_ac() reports the wing's own mean aerodynamic chord and where its aerodynamic center sits relative to the root leading edge. Both come straight from closed-form wing-theory integrals for the linear-taper and elliptical planform, not from a table: c̄ = (2/3)c_root(1+λ+λ²)/(1+λ), x_AC = ȳ·tan(Λ) + 0.25c̄. This only covers the wing's own half of a stability check. A real static margin also needs the aircraft's CG and any tail, which is out of scope for a wing-only script.

Two wing-mass models. --mass-model empirical is a single fitted AR^0.5 exponent. --mass-model beam is inspired by Zhao et al.'s finite-element model updating for a composite flying-wing (AIAA SciTech 2019, 2019-1814), which calibrates mass and stiffness against real vibration-test data. It makes two real structural drivers explicit instead: ultimate load factor and airfoil thickness ratio, through a first-order beam-bending scaling, m ∝ (AR/AR_ref)^1.5 · (n/n_ref) · (t/c_ref ÷ t/c)^0.5. The AR penalty is steeper, load factor enters linearly, and thinner airfoils cost more mass. It's a physically derived scaling, not a named curve fit, so it isn't borrowing anyone else's exact coefficients.

Joint taper search. --objective combined searches taper jointly with cl and aspect ratio, inspired by Bombardieri et al.'s coupled aerostructural wing optimization (Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization, 2021). Their central finding is that optimizing aerodynamics and structure separately misses gains a coupled search finds. Taper's only channel into this model is bending relief to wing mass to hover energy, η_bend = 2(1+2λ)/(3(1+λ)), weighed against induced drag from the Oswald-efficiency estimate, e₀ = 4.61(1−0.045·AR^0.68)cos(Λ)^0.15 − 3.1, C_Di = C_L²/(π·AR·e₀). That's a narrower coupling than the paper's full aero-structural one, but it's real: a taper that trades structural weight for nothing in cruise drag gets evaluated by the same objective as cl and AR, not decided in a separate step.

Sizing the wing

Everything starts from the lift equation. The wing has to carry the lift mass at cruise speed, so the lift coefficient fixes the required area, and the aspect ratio then splits that area into span and chord.

Area, span, and chord
S=2mgρCLv2b=AR·Sc¯=Sb croot=2c¯1+λctip=λcroot(elliptical:croot=4Sπb)

Area scales as 1/v², the same relationship that makes Mission Model's cruise speed matter so much. Mean chord is S/b regardless of taper; taper only changes how that mean splits between root and tip.

The energy objective

The energy objective adds two costs that pull in opposite directions. A higher aspect ratio cuts induced drag, which saves cruise energy. It also makes the wing heavier, and a heavier wing costs more energy to hover. The search finds where those cancel.

Total mission energy for one candidate wing
E=D·v·tcruise+Phover·thover D=12ρv2S(CD0+CDi)CDi=CL2π·AR·e0 Phover=[(m+mwing)g]3/2FM·2ρAdiskAdisk=mdisk loading

The hover term is ideal momentum-theory induced power divided by a figure of merit. FM = 0.6, from a multicopter endurance paper that states typical propellers land between 0.5 and 0.7 (arXiv:2109.04741). The disk is fixed hardware sized once at the baseline mass, so a heavier wing changes the weight the disk lifts, not its area. e₀ is Raymer's fit up to AR 13, and above that I switch to Obert's e₀ = 1/(1.05 + 0.007π·AR), because Raymer's fit crosses zero near AR 18.5. The search is a 100 × 100 grid over CL and AR, with a 20-step taper search added under the combined objective.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Search landscape
The actual (lift coefficient × aspect ratio) energy landscape the optimizer searched for one tier; darker is lower cost. Ring marks the found minimum.
Bending relief vs. taper ratio
η_bend = 2(1+2λ)/(3(1+λ)), computed over the full taper range. This is the one number taper actually moves in the model, weighed against induced drag to find the joint optimum. Marker is the search's real result for the TailSitter Balanced tier, λ = 0.30 → η = 0.82.
Example wing with joint taper search
Real output of --objective combined --taper-min 0.3 --taper-max 1.0 for the TailSitter Balanced tier (92.5 kg lift mass, 18.8 m/s cruise): AR 8.64, taper ratio 0.30 (root 1.151 m / tip 0.345 m chord), span 6.463 m. Marker is the reported aerodynamic center: MAC 0.820 m, 0.205 m aft of the root leading edge, 1.326 m out along the span.
NACA 2412, the file's own --naca example
Computed live from the same closed-form thickness/camber equations naca4_airfoil_point() uses; the exact surface, not a traced shape. Dashed line is the camber line; camber and thickness are what --naca hands to SolidWorks as parametric equations.

Log Dashboard

Live demo →

A Flask + Plotly dashboard that decodes ArduCopter/PX4 flight logs into a full diagnostic report. Upload your own flight log in the live demo and get back the score, the issues list, and every chart. The numbers on this page come from a real sample log.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
Every ArduPilot-based flight controller (Pixhawk and compatibles) writes a binary .BIN log of everything it measured mid-flight, hundreds of message types at up to a few hundred Hz. Reading that raw log to answer "was this flight okay, and if not, why" normally means a separate desktop tool (MAVExplorer) and manual digging. This dashboard does that automatically. Upload a log and get back attitude tracking, vibration spectra, motor balance, PID tracking, GPS track, battery health, and barometer/magnetometer data across dedicated tabs, plus one overall flight-quality verdict.

It's built for the same audience Mission Model is: someone who just flew a real airframe and needs to know whether the motors, frame, or tuning are actually behaving before flying again, not a generic telemetry viewer.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
The backend (python_backend.py) reads a raw .BIN log with pymavlink, walks its message stream, and classifies the airframe from its frame-type parameter (quad/hex/octo/X8/tri/Y3/Y6). Vibration comes from the IMU's three accelerometer axes, and I look at it two ways: how big it is, and what frequency it lives at.

Ten analysis passes run per log: IMU, vibration, attitude, battery, motors, PID/rate controller, GPS, barometer, magnetometer, and discrete flight events (mode changes, arming, errors), each producing its own stats block. A summary pass then scores the flight 0–100 and lists specific issues (e.g. "poor roll stability," "motor sync issues") instead of just dumping charts and leaving the reader to spot problems.

The dashboard (log_dashboard.html) renders the decoded series with Plotly, plus a Custom Plot tab that lets you overlay any two decoded variables against time regardless of category. That's useful for correlating, say, vibration against throttle.

Vibration

I estimate the sample rate from the median gap between timestamps. Size comes from combining the three axes into one magnitude and taking its RMS, which I grade against fixed thresholds. Frequency comes from Welch's method, which averages the spectra of overlapping segments and gives a smoother estimate than one raw FFT, plus a raw FFT to pick out the strongest peak in the 20–500 Hz motor band.

Magnitude, sample rate, and the dominant frequency
|a|=ax2+ay2+az2arms=⟨|a|2⟩fs=106median(Δtµs) X(f)=|ℱ{a(t)}|=|∫a(t)e−i2πftdt|f*=argmax20≤f≤500Xz(f)

arms under 30 m/s² grades good, 30–60 elevated, and above 60 critical. Each Welch segment is about two seconds of samples, never fewer than 256, and I plot the square root of the PSD so the axis reads closer to acceleration units. The Z-axis peak f* is what the dashboard suggests as a notch-filter frequency. This is the same analysis MAVExplorer does for ArduPilot logs, run automatically.

The flight-quality score

The score is a deduction ledger, not a learned model. It starts at 100 and every check that trips subtracts a fixed penalty, so you can always trace a number back to the finding that cost it.

Score and verdict
S=max(0,100−∑ipi)pi∈{5,10,15,20}

Penalties: critical vibration −20 (elevated −10); accelerometer noise above 15 m/s² −10 per axis; attitude error RMS above 5 −5 per axis; voltage sag above 2 V −10; minimum voltage below 10 V −15; motor imbalance above 15% −10; motor sync error above 5 −5; motor correlation below 0.85 −5; rate-controller error RMS above 10 −5 per axis; more than 5 flight events −10. Verdicts: 90 and up Excellent, 75 Good, 60 Fair, 40 Poor, below that Critical. The sample flight lost 35 points across 7 findings and scored 65, Fair.

tabs.html:

Real commanded-vs-actual roll from the sample log's attitude pass. The visible gap between the two lines is what the flight-quality pass is flagging as poor roll stability, not an assumption about the aircraft.

Liquid Rocket

Ground-station software for CWRU's Liquid Propulsion Team, rebuilt from two prototypes that were never actually integrated into one working app, one of them my own original hot-fire GUI.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
On CWRU's Liquid Propulsion Team (Aug 2025 – Jan 2026) I designed the mechanical thrust-control hardware for hot-fire tests, solenoids and servos regulating propellant flow, and built the PyQt5 control GUI that ran the hot-fire sequences against it.

A liquid rocket static test (or hot-fire test) needs a ground station: software running on a laptop near the test stand that shows the person running the test what's happening in real time, tank and chamber pressures, temperatures, thrust (via a load cell), and lets them open or close valves and fire the igniter without touching the hardware directly. Every reading also needs to be logged, since post-test analysis (did the chamber pressure spike, did a valve stick) depends on having the full data, not just what was visible live.

This app is that ground station, rebuilt: a P&ID (piping-and-instrumentation diagram) view for valve control, a live-gauge view for the 9 real sensor channels, and a logging view that records a full test session to CSV.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
The repo held two separate PyQt prototypes on incompatible Qt bindings: my own original PyQt5 data-logging page (main_v2.py) from the actual hot-fire tests, and a separate PyQt6 P&ID valve-control page. Its own readme said as much: "still needs to be integrated with the other page."

I rebuilt it as one PyQt6 app (ground_station/) sharing a single sensor/valve state across three tabs: Controls (the real P&ID diagram plus working valve toggles), Live Data (one gauge per real sensor channel), and Logging (start/stop to the documented raw + interpolated CSV pair).

The wire protocol (P0–P6, T0, L0, one name,value,timestamp line per reading) matches the real Teensy firmware exactly, so a fake data source stands in for hardware without changing anything else. That's verified with a headless smoke test that boots the real window, ticks it, toggles a valve, and checks a logging session actually writes CSVs.

The live demo linked below is a from-scratch JavaScript port of that same protocol and gauge math, not a screen recording. It runs the identical random-walk sensor simulation and the identical SVG gauge/valve drawing code the Python app uses, so what you click there is what the desktop app actually does with no hardware attached.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Data flow
One wire protocol, shared across a fake source (used here) and a future real Teensy connection, feeding all three tabs.
Live Data tab gauge grid
The Live Data tab's real gauge grid: 7 pressure channels, 1 thermocouple, 1 load cell, same P0–P6/T0/L0 IDs the wire protocol and the real Teensy firmware both use.
⚠ Valve toggles are display-only. No serial command channel to real hardware exists yet.

Fly-Brain Drone

A drone whose vision runs through a connectome-constrained model of the fruit fly's optic lobe, with a trained readout that turns the network's activity into steer and speed. Built and tested in a Gazebo simulator, first with a PX4 flight controller and since October 2026 with ArduPilot. Work in progress. In closed loop the decoder alone works partly, and with the semantic layer it works. It also forages on a hunger drive, avoids obstacles from a fly-network cue, and lands on food hidden behind a wall in simulation.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
The idea is a drone whose reflexes come from a model of a fly's visual system instead of a hand-written vision pipeline. A camera frame goes into flyvis, a published connectome-constrained network of the fruit fly's optic lobe, and what comes out is a stream of neuron activity. A small trained readout turns that activity into a steer and a speed, and a flight controller does the actual flying (PX4 at first, ArduPilot since October 2026). A slower vision-language layer is meant to decide what the mission is right now, while the fly-brain reflexes lead the motion.

The test task is deliberately small. A yellow ball, the "food," sits 5–10 m from the drone in a Gazebo Harmonic world with the autopilot running as software-in-the-loop. The drone starts at home facing a random heading and succeeds by getting within 1.5 m of the food inside 60 simulated seconds. That is small enough to measure, and it needs both halves of the stack: seeing the food, and searching when it is out of view.

In the latest comparison, 12 episodes with the same seeds for every policy, the camera-only fly-brain decoder finds the food in 10 of 12, and a PID teacher that is handed the food's true bearing finds it in 12 of 12. The decoder is slow, though: about 23 s to the food against the teacher's 10 s. A plain yellow-blob detector with no brain also gets 12 of 12. So most of this page is about where the decoder falls short and what carries it.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
The stack runs from camera to PX4 setpoint through the chain below. Everything up to the arbiter runs on the host, and only the PX4 bridge and the Gazebo camera live in the Docker container.

Pipeline
Camera to PX4. The fly-brain reflex leads; the slower goal from the semantic layer only gates the mode and caps the speed.

The eye

The flyvis network takes one luminance channel, so colour is invisible to it and the food has to contrast in brightness. I convert each camera frame to luminance, then place it inside the fly's eye at its true angular size. One ommatidium sees 5.8°, drawn 2 px wide on the canvas, so a 99.7° camera image is about 34 px wide, centred on a grey canvas, and the hexals outside the camera's field of view see grey. flyvis samples 721 hexals from that canvas. A quick check in the encoder asserts that the connectome's hexal order matches the sampler's, because a mismatch would silently put the image on the wrong cells.

The network is stateful: one step per camera frame with the state carried between frames, starting from a one-second grey steady state. flyvis was trained at 50 Hz, so each 20 Hz camera frame is split into sub-steps no longer than that.

Luminance, angular size, and sub-stepping
Y=0.299R+0.587G+0.114B w=FOVΔφ/2=99.7°5.8°/2≈34 px n=⌈50 Hzfcam⌉=⌈5020⌉=3 dt=1fcamn=160 s

Δφ is the interommatidial angle of the fly, w the image width in canvas pixels (two per ommatidium), and n the number of network sub-steps per camera frame. The image height follows from the aspect ratio.

The readout

flyvis models only the optic lobe. It has no descending neurons, the cells that carry commands from the fly's brain down to its motor system, so a true descending-neuron readout is not available from it. What I read out instead is the network's own 34 output cell types (the T4/T5 motion cells, Tm, TmY, and so on), the cells that project out of the optic lobe toward the central brain. It is a proxy, and I call it descending-neuron-inspired, not descending-neuron activity.

Each type is mean-pooled over a 3×3 grid of the hex field so left and right, up and down, survive. Averaging a whole type into one number would throw away exactly the geometry a steering signal needs.

Reservoir and ridge readout

Between the network and the decoder sits a fixed random echo-state reservoir. Reservoir computing means the recurrent part is never trained: its random dynamics give the readout a short memory of recent activity, and only a linear layer on top is fit. That memory matters here because the drone's yaw lags its command by about half a second.

Pooled features, reservoir, and ridge readout
uc,r,k=1|Scrk|∑i∈Scrkai u~t=ut−μs xt=(1−α)xt−1+α⁢tanh(Winu~t+Wxt−1) W=ρW0|λmax(W0)| φt=[u~t;xt] y^t=Θφt+b Θ=argmin∑t‖yt−Θφt‖2+λ‖Θ‖F2

c is one of 34 output cell types and (r, k) a cell of the 3×3 grid, so u has 34 × 9 = 306 entries and φ has 306 + 500 = 806. The reservoir has 500 units, leak α = 0.3, spectral radius ρ = 0.9, 10% connection density, and input weights uniform in ±0.1, all fixed. A single global scale s is used instead of per-feature standardisation, which amplified the near-silent cells: held-out z-scores reached 70. y is (steer, speed, confidence), and λ is picked per target from {1, 10, 10², 10³, 10⁴} by 5-fold cross-validation.

The teacher, and what the decoder can learn

A decoder needs something to imitate, so a PID teacher with ground-truth food bearing and range produces the reflex the decoder is trained toward. The teacher flies randomized episodes with Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise added to the steer that is sent to the drone (σ = 0.5, τ = 1 s), so the camera sees off-centre views, while the training labels stay the clean teacher output.

Teacher reflex from ground-truth bearing error
e=θfood−ψheading steer=clip(kpe+kde˙,−1,1) speed=max(0,1−|e|45°)⋅clip(r−13,0.15,1)

e is positive when the food is to the right, r is the range to the food in metres, kp = 0.0333 (full steer at a 30° error) and kd = 0.005 (the integral gain is zero). Speed goes to zero at a 45° error, so the drone turns in place before it drives, and falls toward a floor of 0.15 as it closes on the food. The teacher's confidence is simply whether the food is visible in the image.

Here is what the decoder can and cannot learn. Steer and speed are trained only on frames where the food is actually in the image, because elsewhere the teacher's "turn toward the food" comes from ground truth the eye can't see. Confidence is trained on all frames, class-balanced, since about 80% of the first frames had the food visible and a plain fit just predicts "visible." Every fit is scored on held-out episodes, never held-out frames of episodes it trained on.

DAgger

A decoder trained only on teacher-driven flights has never seen the search phase or its own mistakes. DAgger fixes that: the decoder drives a fraction of the episodes, the teacher labels every frame anyway, and the fit runs over the aggregate. Round 1 used 36 episodes, with the decoder driving 70% of them, for 25,300 frames including the original teacher data.

Arbiter and the semantic layer

The arbiter fuses the fast reflex with a cached slow goal into a PX4 velocity setpoint. I made the fly-brain lead: its reflex drives the motion, and the goal is advisory, gating the mode (HOLD and ABORT stop, SEARCH and INSPECT slow the drone) and capping speed. An active obstacle veto in the reflex beats any goal, a stale goal falls back to SEARCH after 3 s, and an invalid reflex produces a zero setpoint so the 20 Hz OFFBOARD stream never stalls, which PX4 would answer by disarming.

Reflex to velocity setpoint
ψ˙=60 °/s⋅steer vx=2 m/s⋅speed⋅cap cap=min(capgoal,capmode)

The mode caps are 0.3 in SEARCH, 0.15 in INSPECT, and 0 in HOLD and ABORT. In SEARCH, if the reflex confidence is below 0.2 or the goal says the target is unseen, the drone yaws at a fixed 20°/s to scan.

The semantic layer has two forms so far. CvVLM is a model-free stand-in that finds the food's yellow blob in the image and reports its bearing and range from pixels alone with a pinhole model and the food's known size. That same detector drives the camera-only baseline, the fair comparison for the fly-brain decoder: same camera, same PID, no brain. HostedVLM calls a hosted vision-language model with the image, the mission and the decoded reflex, and repairs malformed output once before falling back to HOLD. It has been tested against fake transports only, never the live API.

Bearing and range from a yellow blob
f=W/2tan(FOV/2) θ=arctancx−(W−1)/2f r=f⋅Rρpx,ρpx=Aπ

W is the image width in pixels, cx the centre of the blob's bounding box (robust to an occluded edge), A its pixel area, and R = 0.4 m the food's real radius. This uses no ground truth.

The simulator

The results above this section ran on PX4 SITL and Gazebo Harmonic, headless in Docker with software rendering, which is slow: about 0.6× real time, so every timestamp in the stack is sim time taken from the camera frame stamps. Worse, the real-time factor halves after about six minutes of container uptime, even with no client attached. The fix was to run short chunks on freshly started sims, up to three in parallel with isolated Gazebo partitions, which gives about 3× the throughput. Caching the JSON-schema validators cut the policy step from 20 ms to about 8 ms.

Moving to ArduPilot

In October 2026 I replaced PX4 with ArduPilot (ArduCopter 4.6.3 SITL with ardupilot_gazebo). PX4's simulator lost about a quarter of attempts to attitude, yaw or compass faults and fly-aways, ArduPilot takes the Matek optical-flow and range sensor I plan to fly natively, and the VTOL team's own tools are ArduCopter. A spike came first. The simulated drone armed on all 13 of 13 fresh boots, and a zero vertical-speed command in GUIDED mode held altitude by itself (1.98 m to 1.98 m over 10 sim-seconds), so the height-hold controller I had written for PX4 could be deleted. The cost is speed: with both cameras running ArduPilot's sim ran at about 0.28× real time, roughly 15% slower than PX4.

The bridge now goes GUIDED, arm, takeoff, then streams body-frame velocity. Precision landing sends the downward camera's view of the food to the autopilot as angles, not as a position:

Landing-target angles
θx=atan2(right,down)θy=atan2(forward,down)

Both are sent in the body frame with the range set to the height above the box. With a ground-truth feed, a test that hovered at 2 m and moved the food 2 m east touched down 0.00 m from it, against a PX4 median of 0.065 m. I checked the signs live before trusting it.

The autopilot now owns the safety nets. A 10 m circle fence brakes the drone 2 m short of the edge, and when the onboard computer's heartbeat stops, ArduPilot lands the drone about two seconds later. Both were verified in the simulator. A QGroundControl companion starts the flights from the ground station: you draw the search box with four clicks on the map. I tested the companion through scripted operators, not by clicking in QGroundControl itself.

I re-ran the wall mission on 12 seeds, fenced, on the new stack. The first pass landed 9 of 12 within 0.04 m of the food, with 0 collisions on each landing. Seeds 4, 5 and 8 hit the sheets (2, 7 and 3 times) and landed 1.2 to 1.7 m away. The logs showed why. The avoider's escape was a nudge: about 1 m/s sideways for about 1 s, then it released and drove straight back at the same obstacle. The cue was firing every frame at 20 Hz without gaps, so checking more often was not the fix. Simply triggering earlier did not help either: with the trigger lowered to 0.25 all three still failed, with 2, 2 and 5 hits.

So I rewrote the escape as a committed reflex. It runs at 2 m/s with a reverse component to kill the forward momentum, it holds for at least 1.5 s and keeps going 1.5 s after the view clears, it also fires when the obstacle strength rises fast in a single frame, and the forward brake can go down to 10% speed. Re-running the three failing seeds, seeds 4 and 8 landed 0.03 m from the food with one hit each, and seed 5 still failed with 5 hits. Seeds 6 and 7 still landed with no hits. That makes 11 of 12 landed, but it mixes old and new settings, because I only re-ran the five seeds I changed things for. The remaining hits are at the outer corner of the alcove, against the fence edge. The white sheets seen edge-on barely register as dark there (strength about 0.15 against a trigger of 0.3), so the fly-network cue does not see them coming. A second cue, or keeping the search route away from the fence, is the next fix.

The same stack also runs a cleaner mission with no avoider: take off, find the box, land on top of it. With the colour detector on the downward camera it landed on the box in 3 of 3 runs, 0.03 to 0.05 m from the centre. With a small downward-camera YOLO detector trained from scratch on simulator frames (yolov8n, validation mAP50 0.995 on the same hover runs, so optimistic), 7 of 8 seeds landed on top, and the 0.07 m results sit close to my 0.076 m limit.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
The offline readout experiments come first, on 26 teacher episodes with held-out-episode cross-validation. The reservoir helps: steer R² goes from 0.23 to 0.31. Reservoir size, input scale and leak barely matter. Widening the readout from the 34 output types to all 65 flyvis cell types does not help (0.30). Pooling to 1×5 instead of 3×3 does about the same. And raw retina luminance is much worse than the fly-network features, at 0.16–0.18 against 0.31–0.33 with the same reservoir, so the connectome-constrained front end is adding information. A nonlinear model (ExtraTrees) on the same features only reaches about 0.49, so the features, not the linear readout, are the limit. In that first fit the sign of the steer agreed with the teacher 77% of the time, speed R² was 0.58, and food-visible accuracy was 0.88 against a majority baseline of 0.83.

What limits the readout
Held-out-episode steer R² from the offline sweep on 26 teacher episodes. The red bar is the configuration I kept. The nonlinear model uses the same features as the linear one, which is why I read the ceiling as being in the features.

The first closed-loop test, with the teacher-only decoder, is where it falls apart. On the same 10 randomized scenarios, the PID teacher succeeded 10 of 10 with a mean of 9.6 s to the food, and the camera-only decoder succeeded 4 of 10, with a mean of 17.1 s on the four that made it. Neither collided with anything. The decoder succeeded in 3 of the 5 scenarios where the food started in view and 1 of the 5 where it did not.

Two things explain it. First, the decoder's confidence does not tell "food visible" from "not visible" in the loop: it averages 0.68 when the food is visible and 0.62 when it is not, an accuracy of 0.43, against 0.88 in cross-validation. So it stays in APPROACH and never scans. Second, its steer is only weakly right when it does see the food, with sign agreement of 62% and a steer R² of −0.22 against the teacher's reflex. The flyvis output cells are motion-driven, so a food that sits near the image centre during a pursuit is a weak cue, and the yaw lag means the optic flow reflects commands that are already half a second old.

One scenario, two flights
Top-down ground-truth track of scenario 2 from the closed-loop runs: the PID teacher reaches the food in 8.5 s, while the decoder wanders for the full 60 s and gets no closer than 4.5 m. The dashed circle is the 1.5 m success radius.

DAgger round 1 was the first response. On-policy, the decoder succeeded in 9 of the 26 episodes it drove to completion, and the held-out fit of the refit decoder has steer R² 0.31 (sign agreement 76%), speed R² 0.48, and food-visible accuracy 0.82 against a 0.62 majority baseline. Food was visible in 38% of the frames, against about 80% before, so the data now includes the search phase the first version never saw.

DAgger round 2 repeated this with the round-1 decoder driving 80% of the episodes, on three parallel sims. The final fit uses 97 episodes and 46.5k frames, with food visible in 44% of them. The held-out fit did not improve: steer R² 0.27 (sign agreement 79%), speed R² 0.25 and food-visible accuracy 0.78 against a 0.56 majority baseline, where round 1 had 0.31, 0.48 and 0.82. The data now holds more of the decoder's own mistakes, so the folds are harder and the numbers are not directly comparable, but the readout metric did not get better.

The final closed-loop comparison ran every policy on the same 12 seeds, three fresh sims in parallel, with a 35 s timeout (the first test used 60 s). The round-2 decoder reached the food in 10 of 12 episodes, a mean of 23.1 s on the ones that succeeded, with no collisions. The first, teacher-only decoder got 4 of 10 on its own scenarios, so I re-ran it, and the no-reservoir variant, on these same 12 seeds. The teacher-only decoder gets 4 of 12, so the DAgger rounds are what took it from 4 to 10 (Fisher exact p = 0.04). Removing the reservoir gives 9 of 12 against 10 of 12, which is no detectable difference at this sample size, in line with the offline sweep where the reservoir moved steer R² only from 0.23 to 0.31.

Success over 12 matched episodes
Same 12 seeds for every policy, 35 s timeout. Mean time to food: PID teacher 9.9 s, pixel-only baseline 13.7 s, decoder alone 23.1 s, decoder plus goal 20.6 s, decoder without a goal 30.2 s, and 14.9 s and 22.3 s for the two ablations, the teacher-data-only decoder and the no-reservoir one. The goal here comes from the CvVLM stand-in, not a hosted model.

The semantic layer is what carries the search. The same decoder plus the CvVLM goal got 12 of 12, and with the goal removed, so the arbiter falls back on a stale goal, it got 6 of 12. A goal that says the target is unseen is what makes the drone scan, which the decoder's own confidence never could.

This is also where the result stops flattering the fly brain. The pixel-only baseline, a yellow-blob detector feeding the same PID with no brain, got 12 of 12 in 13.7 s with one collision, faster than both the decoder and the full stack. Twelve episodes is a small sample: 10 of 12 against 12 of 12 is not a real difference, but 6 of 12 against 12 of 12 is. On this task the connectome-constrained front end adds information offline, in the steer R² gap over raw pixels, but it has not yet turned that into better flying than classical vision does.

About one chunk in twelve failed for infrastructure reasons, either the sim not coming up or the drone not taking off. I re-ran those on fresh sims instead of counting them as policy failures.

tabs.label: Hunger, a wall and a landing
tabs.html:
The pixel baseline already gets 12 of 12 on open ground, so the fly network needs a task where seeing a coloured ball is not enough. I moved the food 2 m behind an obstacle on the line from home and ran the same pixel-only policy, with no avoidance, on 12 seeds. It reached the food in 5 of 12 and had 15 collisions, and all five successes flew into the obstacle first. None of the seven failures got within 7.8 m of the food. The reason was the search: when the obstacle hides the food the old behaviour was a scan, about 0.6 m/s forward while yawing 20°/s, which is a circle of roughly 1.7 m radius around the start. That is not a search.

Hunger

I replaced the scan with a drive. A hunger value h between 0 and 1 rises while no food is in view and drains when it is, and it sets how far and how fast the drone forages. Foraging is a loop: a full 360° turn on the spot, because the forward camera is the only sensor; then the compass heading with the least-visited ground in a 2 m grid; then a run toward it; then another turn. A 14 m leash keeps it near where it started. It starts at 0.5 so it moves from the first frame, and it reaches full hunger after 50 s without food. This is a state variable in the controller, not part of the fly network: the network does not do the searching.

Hunger and the foraging run
h←min(1,h+0.02Δt) h←max(0,h−0.2Δt) L=4+4h v=0.5+0.7h

The first line applies with no food in view, the second with food in view. L is the run length in metres and v the run speed in m/s.

What the network can see of an obstacle

The obvious cue is looming, so I tested it before building on it. I recorded five of the pixel-only episodes: 5,390 frames, 1,696 of them "obstacle within 4 m, within 40° of the optical axis, closing faster than 0.3 m/s". Each cue is scored by how well it separates those frames from the rest (AUC, where 0.5 is chance). A radial-expansion readout from the T4/T5 motion cells scored 0.50, and classical optical-flow divergence scored 0.38. The world is flat ground under a grey sky with one dark blob, so the motion cells fire on the blob's edges only, and a yaw turn sweeps those edges sideways: expansion cannot be told from rotation. What did work was the OFF pathway in the centre of the view, with T1, Tm5a, Tm5b and Tm9 up and T2, T3, Tm3 and TmY9 down when a dark object fills the middle, at 0.87. That is a proximity cue, not looming.

It reads apparent size, not distance, so an 8 m wall scores as high at 2 to 4 m as a pole does under 1 m. I recalibrated the trigger with ray-cast distance from one wall mission: the score is −1.41 at 6 to 9 m, −1.24 at 4 to 6 m, −1.10 at 2 to 4 m and −0.88 under 1 m, against a median of −1.72 with no wall ahead. The reflex slows as the score rises and, at a normalised strength of 0.45 (score −1.0, about 2 m from the wall), strafes away from the dark side with yaw held until the centre column has been clear for a second. My first version dodged on a fixed 2 s timer and drove back into the wall. I also tried letting the left and right columns fire the veto, since a wall approached at an angle sits there: it landed 2 of 5 against 5 of 6 for centre-only, with the same total hits, so it is off.

Landing on top of it

The mission originally glided down on a range estimate from the blob's width. On the wall runs that estimate came out about 2× too high at 3 to 6 m, and the food left the camera's narrow vertical view while the mission still believed it was 5 m away, so it never made the last approach. The best of the first three usable runs landed 3.45 m from the food. I replaced it with a glide that needs neither range nor altitude: hold the food's image row at a fixed angle below the optical axis. On 1,475 logged frames with ground truth the blob row is 76 tan δ − 0.9 px (residual 5.5 px), where δ is the depression angle. Holding δ at 14° makes the height above the food fall in proportion to distance, so at about 0.6 m height the drone is about 0.8 m out. The short creep and PX4's own landing do the rest.

The cause of the bad range turned out to be one constant. The blob-width model had a +5 px padding term fitted at short range. Refit on 10,759 frames against ground truth it is −2.5 px (width = 69.5 / slant − 2.5), which moves the ratio of estimated to true range from 1.3 at 1.5 to 3 m, 1.8 at 3 to 5 m and 2.7 at 5 to 8 m to 0.92 to 1.02 across the whole span. I also stopped using PX4's altitude in the range: it drifts from the simulator's true height by up to +1.3 m and −0.6 m over flights longer than 100 s, so horizontal distance is now slant × cos δ, with δ from the image row.

Elevation-locked glide
r=fytanδ+b h−0.4=dtanδ∗ vz=−vxtanδ∗−k(δ−δ∗)

r is the food's image row measured from the centre, with fy = 76 px and b = −0.9 px fitted from the logs. h is the drone's height, 0.4 m is the food's centre height, d the horizontal distance and δ* = 14° the locked angle. The last line is the vertical speed: a feed-forward from the forward speed plus a correction with k = 2.0 m/s per radian.

The wall test

An 8 m wall stands 6 m east of home and the food is 9 m east, so from home the wall hides it completely. The drone starts on the ground, takes off, searches, glides down and lands, and it counts as a success if it touches down within 1.0 m of the food. Before the elevation lock, none of the three usable runs landed within 1.0 m: the best was 3.45 m with two collisions, and the others timed out. With the lock, the first batch of seven runs (fixed search seed, four with the avoider and three without) landed within 1.0 m five times, at 0.23 to 0.69 m. With the search seed changed on every run, six paired missions landed centre-only five times out of six, at 0.23 to 0.49 m. The one miss got within 0.7 m and never triggered the landing.

With the range fixed I ran the avoider on and off on the same seeds, one run each, in three batches of six. Every touchdown was about 0.7 m short at first, which was my own landing hand-off radius; at 0.35 m the landings came down to 0.15 to 0.54 m from the food. Wall hits are the noisy part. On seeds 1 to 6 the avoider hit the wall once and the no-avoider runs hit it 16 times; on seeds 7 to 12 it was 5 against 3; on seeds 13 to 18, 5 against 8. Over all 18 seeds that is 11 hits with the avoider (0.61 a run) and 27 without (1.50 a run). The avoider had fewer hits in 8 of the 18 pairs, more in 4 and tied in 6. A sign test on those pairs gives p = 0.39 and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which also weighs how big each difference is, gives p = 0.046. Landing within 1.0 m was 16 of 18 with the avoider and 17 of 18 without, and crash-free landings were 9 against 7 (p = 0.74). So it hits the wall less on average, but the evidence is weak and comes mostly from the first six seeds.

The two avoider runs that failed both happened near other obstacles. The wall scene also holds the world's four original obstacles, including a 3 m box against the wall's west face and a 4 m pole, and a sideways strafe along the wall can run into them. In one run the drone passed about a metre from the pole, lost 0.6 m of height in under a second and landed 3.96 m from the food. In the other it tumbled near the north end of the wall and ended up on the ground 46 m away.

One wall, three flights
Top-down ground-truth tracks of three wall missions: one with the range-model glide, then two with the elevation lock. The two lock flights use the same code and differ only in the search seed. The drone starts at home facing north; the wall and food are drawn to scale.

The obstacle suite tells a different story. On the 12 blocked-path seeds the old pixel-only baseline got 5 of 12 with 15 collisions. Hunger alone got 9 of 9 with 1 collision (three seeds were skipped after repeated sim faults), so the search fix, not the network, is what turned that scenario around. Adding the avoider gave 8 of 12 with 5 collisions, and on the nine shared seeds 6 of 9 against 9 of 9, which is not a significant difference (p about 0.2). Its failed episodes had almost no avoider vetoes, so I read them as search-route luck under a 60 s timeout. On the wall its benefit is small and uneven, and here it added nothing.

What I can not say yet is how far this goes. A wall hit here is an entry into the wall's footprint plus a 0.35 m margin, so some are near-misses; it is one scene with 18 runs per arm; and about one attempt in four hit a sim fault (no frame, or no takeoff) during this work, partly from macOS background load and once from my own analysis running alongside. I re-ran those and did not count them as results.

tabs.label: Next
tabs.html:
The next step is a harder scene for the network's own cue. This world is flat ground under a grey sky, so the motion cells have nothing to fire on except the edges of one dark object; several walls, a pole field and a textured floor would test whether the T4/T5 expansion readout can carry looming when there is something to see. Before that, a look at the two avoider runs that crashed or landed far from the food, and a longer timeout on the blocked-path suite. After that, the landing depends on a forward camera that loses the food in the last metre, so a downward camera is the real fix on hardware. One loose end: HostedVLM still has not met the live API. The geofence now exists in the autopilot. Still missing before hardware: the rest of the ArduPilot re-validation (avoider against no avoider, the six-seed landing table with the real downward detector), flying the Matek flow sensor, and a timing test on a Jetson. First, the outer-corner hits on the wall mission.

⚠ Simulation only. The semantic layer has run only as a pixel-based stand-in and against fake transports, not against a live vision-language model, and the readout is a descending-neuron-inspired proxy, not real descending neurons. The wall and obstacle results come from one scene, 18 wall runs per arm on PX4 and 12 on ArduPilot. The avoider hit the wall less on average but the evidence is weak and uneven between batches, and on the blocked-path suite hunger alone does the work.

← All projects

NACA to SolidWorks

Open the tool →

Type a NACA 4- or 5-digit airfoil and a chord length, and it downloads XYZ point files for SolidWorks' Curve Through XYZ Points. It does the whole calculation in your browser, so there's nothing to install and nothing uploaded.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
SolidWorks has no built-in NACA airfoil generator. You either trace one from a picture or paste coordinates in from a website you hope is right. I wanted the exact surface, at whatever chord the part needs, without leaving the browser. So the page evaluates the NACA equations directly and writes the points out as tab-separated X Y Z text, which is the format Curve Through XYZ Points reads. The curve lands in the Front plane at Z = 0.

It downloads three files: the upper surface, the lower surface, or one closed loop running tail, nose, tail. The chord you type is the scale, and the units are whatever your SolidWorks document uses.

I built it as the manual counterpart to Wing Optimizer, which writes the same kind of geometry out as equations. This one is for the moment you just need one airfoil.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
Thickness and surface points

Every NACA airfoil is a camber line with a thickness distribution wrapped around it, perpendicular to the camber line. For thickness fraction t (the last two digits, over 100), the thickness at chordwise station x is a fixed polynomial. The surface points shift each station up and down by yt along the camber line's local normal.

Thickness, then upper and lower surface
yt=5t(0.2969x−0.1260x−0.3516x2+0.2843x3−0.1036x4) θ=arctandycdx xu,l=x∓ytsinθ yu,l=yc±ytcosθ

The published polynomial ends in −0.1015x⁴, which leaves the tail slightly open. At the trailing edge the bracket is 0.2969 − 0.1260 − 0.3516 + 0.2843 − 0.1015 = 0.0021, so a 12% airfoil is 0.00126 of a chord thick there. CAD wants one sharp tail point, so I use −0.1036. The bracket then sums to zero and the surfaces meet exactly. Points are cosine spaced, x = ½(1 − cos(πi/79)), 80 per surface, which puts them densest at the nose where the curvature is.

The camber line

For 4-digit airfoils, the first digit is maximum camber m (over 100) and the second is its position p (over 10). The camber line is two parabolas that meet at x = p with matching slope.

4-digit camber line
yc=mp2(2px−x2)for x < p yc=m(1−p)2((1−2p)+2px−x2)for x ≥ p

The 5-digit series is different. The first digit fixes the design lift coefficient at 0.15 times the digit, so 2xxxx is 0.3. The next two digits give the position of maximum camber and whether the camber line is standard (2p0) or reflex (2p1). The camber line is a cubic whose constants r, k₁, and k₂/k₁ come from NACA's published table, and one expression covers both variants by setting k₂/k₁ to zero for the standard line.

I didn't want to type that table in and trust it. Thin-airfoil theory gives the ideal lift coefficient of any camber line as Cl,i = 2∫ (dyc/dx) cos θ dθ with x = ½(1 − cos θ), so every 2xx line in the table should come out at 0.300. I integrated each one numerically. 230, 240, and 250 give 0.300, and 220 gives 0.302. 210 gives 0.308 and the reflex lines run 0.301 to 0.305, which is the rounding in NACA's published constants and not a transcription error. Together the constants sit within 3% of the target.

6-series and other families need a numerical solve for their camber lines. The tool says it doesn't support them instead of guessing.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
NACA 2412, camber line dashed
Computed live from the same thickness and camber equations the tool uses. This preview draws the published −0.1015 coefficient, so its tail is open by 0.00126 chord. The downloaded points use −0.1036 and close it.
Open the tool →

Flexural Fatigue Test Machine

A flexural fatigue test machine for internal testing, built to ASTM F1387 A6. I designed, manufactured, and implemented it as a Mechanical Engineering Co-Op at Tylok International.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
The machine is for internal testing, built in accordance with ASTM standards to handle a variety of parts and sizes. I owned it end to end: the design, the machining and assembly, and the verification. The test load is over 2,000 lb and the cycle range is over 80,000. The photo shows the assembled machine, with the ASTM F1387 A6 flexure-fatigue label on its controller.

I also developed other internal stress and verification apparatus: thermal, flow, tensile, and pressure testing.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.html:
Stress analysis first. I used fundamental principles of stress analysis to decide how to design the system and what its size constraints were, before any CAD.

CAD. With the approach and the size limits set, I moved into CAD.

Machining and assembly. I machined the parts and assembled the machine.

Verification. I verified the machine with strain gauge readings and the data I collected, and confirmed the results against them.

Data collection and control. I researched, acquired, and integrated a Dewesoft system for data acquisition. I wrote Dewesoft programs (DewesoftX and C++) to collect and analyse the data and to run the machine's control system.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Flexural fatigue machine
The machine as built: two opposed air cylinders on either side of the test fixture, and a controller box with a display and mode switch.

X-8 Tailsitter

An adaptation of the Hexacopter Drone into an X-8 tailsitter frame, focused on generating lift from a wing and a high thrust-to-weight ratio.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html: Designed as a derivative of the hexacopter platform. Rather than six rotors on a flat frame, the X-8 layout pairs eight motors (coaxial or square-8 arrangement) beneath a wing so the airframe can pitch over into wing-borne cruise. The design goal is a high thrust-to-weight ratio so the vehicle can still transition and recover reliably even before the wing is generating full lift.

Quadcopter

I use a basic quadcopter build to teach newer VTOL members multirotor design fundamentals before they move on to transitioning airframes.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html: A standard 5-inch quadcopter frame (four arms, four motors, no wing or transition mechanism) used as the entry point for members who haven't designed a multirotor before. Getting comfortable with a basic frame, motor mount, and landing-gear layout here is what makes the added complexity of Tail Sitter Designs and Tilt Rotor Designs approachable later.

Tail Sitter Designs

An ongoing project: I'm teaching newer VTOL members how to design their own tail sitters, so the club can design successful transition drones.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html:
Tail-sitters are the simplest wing-based VTOL transition mechanism. The whole airframe pitches over rather than tilting individual motors or wing sections, which makes them the right starting point for members who haven't designed a transitioning aircraft before. The current design under review is a biplane tail-sitter: a small quadcopter core with foils that double as landing gear, weighing an S1223 airfoil against NACA 4412/6412 candidates.

Design decisions worked through with the team include 2 vs. 4 rotors, one wing vs. two, and how the wings attach to the frame (a matching profile clamp, bolted to the frame). Transition logic gets validated in PX4 + Gazebo SITL simulation before any hardware flies.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Transition mechanism
CAD not yet finalized; diagram of the mechanism being designed around: the whole airframe pitches from hover to cruise as one rigid body, no separate tilt actuator.

head:
← All projects

Tilt Rotor Designs

Similar to Tail Sitter Designs. I teach newer VTOL members how to design tilt rotors and build their own within a semester.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html: Where a tail-sitter pitches the whole airframe, a tilt-rotor only rotates the motors from vertical to near-horizontal, letting the fuselage stay level through the transition. That's more mechanically complex than a tail-sitter, but easier on payloads and sensors that need to stay upright. It's the natural next step once members have a tail-sitter under their belt.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Transition mechanism
CAD not yet finalized; diagram of the mechanism being designed around: only the rotor nacelles rotate, the fuselage stays level so payloads and sensors don't have to.

DARPA Lift 2028

A drone built to compete in the DARPA LIFT '28 challenge. The current design is a tail sitter with a low rotor count, being actively adapted.

tabs.label: Overview
tabs.html: The CAD counterpart to Mission Model, which sweeps motor/prop/battery combinations against a mock DARPA Heavy Lift 2028 mission. This is the physical airframe that mission analysis is meant to inform. Current direction is a low-rotor-count tail sitter, prioritizing hover efficiency and cruise range for the heavy-lift mission profile over the redundancy a higher rotor count would buy.

tabs.label: Outcome
tabs.html:
Rotor-count trade-off
CAD not yet finalized; the actual design trade-off driving the current direction: 2 rotors over 6, trading redundancy for hover efficiency and cruise range on the heavy-lift mission.
